lesson.title: Liturgical hymn forms and the eight tones

readings.title: Tone I: resurrection hymn
readings.text: While the stone was sealed by the Jews, and soldiers stood on guard over thy body undefiled, thou didst rise on the third day, O Saviour, who givest life unto the world. For which cause the Heavenly Powers cried aloud unto thee, O Giver of Life: Glory to thy resurrection, O Christ! Glory to thy kingdom! Glory to thy providence, O thou who alone lovest mankind!

readings.title: Tone VIII: resurrection hymn
readings.text: Thou didst descend from on high, O Tender-hearted One; thou didst endure the three-days' burial, that thou mightest free us from our passions, O our Life and Resurrection. Glory, O Lord, to thee.

readings.title: Enumeration of the illustrious men in the Church who in their writings have used the word "with."
readings.locator: On the Holy Spirit, chapter XXIX; opening selection
readings.text: 71. In answer to the objection that the doxology in the form "with the Spirit" has no written authority, we maintain that if there is no other instance of that which is unwritten, then this must not be received. But if the greater number of our mysteries are admitted into our constitution without written authority, then, in company with the many others, let us receive this one. For I hold it apostolic to abide also by the unwritten traditions. "I praise you," it is said, "that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances as I delivered them to you;" and "Hold fast the traditions which ye have been taught whether by word, or our Epistle." One of these traditions is the practice which is now before us, which they who ordained from the beginning, rooted firmly in the churches, delivering it to their successors, and its use through long custom advances pace by pace with time. If, as in a Court of Law, we were at a loss for documentary evidence, but were able to bring before you a large number of witnesses, would you not give your vote for our acquittal? I think so; for "at the mouth of two or three witnesses shall the matter be established." And if we could prove clearly to you that a long period of time was in our favour, should we not have seemed to you to urge with reason that this suit ought not to be brought into court against us? For ancient dogmas inspire a certain sense of awe, venerable as they are with a hoary antiquity. I will therefore give you a list of the supporters of the word (and the time too must be taken into account in relation to what passes unquestioned). For it did not originate with us. How could it? We, in comparison with the time during which this word has been in vogue, are, to use the words of Job, "but of yesterday." I myself, if I must speak of what concerns me individually, cherish this phrase as a legacy left me by my fathers. It was delivered to me by one who spent a long life in the service of God, and by him I was both baptized, and admitted to the ministry of the church. While examining, so far as I could, if any of the blessed men of old used the words to which objection is now made, I found many worthy of credit both on account of their early date, and also a characteristic in which they are unlike the men of to-day--because of the exactness of their knowledge.

overview.text: The two resurrection hymns illustrate texts assigned to different tones. A tone is a named musical category in the service tradition; the supplied texts identify Tones I and VIII without providing musical notation. Basil’s separate reading explains the inherited language of praise to the Holy Spirit.

readings.title: The resurrection hymn assigned to Tone I

paragraphs.text: This hymn sets the sealed tomb and its guards beside Christ’s resurrection on the third day. It identifies Christ as the giver of life and places heavenly praise in response to that event. The text provides the hymn’s theological content, rather than instructions for singing its melody.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: The resurrection hymn assigned to Tone VIII

paragraphs.text: The shorter hymn joins Christ’s descent and burial with liberation from the passions, the faults that hold a person in bondage. It identifies Christ himself as life and resurrection. Its assigned tone distinguishes its place in the collection from the preceding hymn.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How Basil explains an inherited expression of praise

paragraphs.text: Basil defends praising God “with the Spirit” by appealing to received apostolic traditions and earlier witnesses. He argues that the expression was handed down rather than newly invented by him. Doxology means an expression of praise; his discussion concerns the theological wording of that praise.
